text: The real test of fluency in two tools isn't writing each one in isolation — it's translating the same algorithm between them and being able to point to exactly where each design decision in one tool maps to a design decision in the other. This capstone does that with a Bell-state circuit, small enough to verify completely.

Four things this capstone covers: a full Qiskit implementation of Bell-state preparation and measurement, the equivalent full Q# implementation, the exact translation decisions at each step — registers, gate calls, measurement — and a verified confirmation that both produce the identical theoretical output distribution.

In Qiskit, QuantumCircuit with 2 and 2 declares a quantum register and a classical register up front, as part of constructing the circuit object. Then h on qubit zero, cx from zero to one, and measure writes results into the classical register at specified indices, read out later from the circuit's results object.

In Q#, use with a tuple allocates both qubits dynamically, scoped to the operation — there's no separate classical register to declare at all, because the measured Result values are just ordinary typed values. H and CNOT take effect immediately when executed, with no intermediate append-to-a-list step, because there's no list. And the operation simply returns the measured Results directly as its typed return value.

Rather than trust the translation by inspection alone, the theoretical distribution was computed directly: starting from |00>, applying H then CNOT via matrix multiplication gives amplitude one over root two on |00> and on |11>, and exactly zero amplitude on |01> and |10>. Squaring gives probability exactly 0.5 for 00, exactly 0.5 for 11, and exactly zero for the other two. Both versions implement precisely this same sequence, so both are consistent with this one independently verified result.

Three decisions map cleanly across both tools: register declaration becomes dynamic qubit allocation, gate methods on a circuit object become direct operation calls that execute immediately, and writing to a classical register becomes simply returning a typed value. Porting this circuit is close to mechanical — what it makes visible is where each tool's design philosophy shows up, even in a two-gate example.

Last lesson turns everything from this comparative project into an actual decision framework — not a recap of features, but a real tool for answering which one you'd reach for on a project in front of you.
